result.summary: Pass Bitcoin Core's compiler and linker hardening flags to the embedded libsecp256k1 build. The change factors hardening flags into a dedicated CMake interface library (`hardening_interface`) linked by `core_interface` and forwards those options to the secp256k1 subtree configuration.
result.problem: The secp256k1 subtree does not inherit flags from `core_interface`, leaving its compiled objects without hardening flags such as stack protection, stack clash protection, and control-flow integrity flags. Because linkers omit binary-wide control-flow protection markers (like AArch64 BTI/PAC or x86_64 CET) if even a single linked object lacks them, the missing flags strip control-flow protections from the final executable on toolchains that do not enable them by default.
evidence: PR description: 'On aarch64 Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15 this also costs the whole binary its control flow property: master's bitcoind has no AArch64 feature note, and the three secp256k1 objects are the only ones in the build tree without it.'
PR description: 'With it, the same build shows AArch64 feature: BTI, PAC, GCS on bitcoind.'
result.card: This pull request passes Bitcoin Core's compiler hardening flags to the embedded libsecp256k1 build by separating them into a reusable CMake interface target. The secp256k1 subtree was previously built without flags such as stack protection and control-flow protection. Because linkers require all linked object files to support control-flow integrity to mark the binary as protected, secp256k1 objects prevented the final executable from having hardware-assisted control-flow protection notes on systems like AArch64 Linux. On Ubuntu 26.04 with GCC 15, this change restores the binary's AArch64 BTI, PAC, and GCS feature markers.

risk.why: Incorrect compiler or linker hardening flags could cause compilation failures across supported toolchains or introduce subtle runtime miscompilations in cryptographic code.
